title: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa
sub: in, ad, ex, cum: places, and Caesar
can: Say where things are and where people are going, then read Caesar's famous first line.
doneText: You can now tell staying from going, use in, ad, ex and cum, and you've read Caesar himself.

discover.intro: Both colours use the same little word, in. Spot why the ending after it changes.

groups.label: Blue
lines: The girl is walking in the street.
The slaves are working in the town.

groups.label: Orange
lines: The girl walks into the street.
The slaves walk into the town.

discover.question: Why vīllā in blue but vīllam in orange?
options: Blue is where someone is (ending -ā or -ō). Orange is movement into a place (ending -am or -um).
Blue is one person, orange is several.
Blue is the past tense, orange the present.
discover.nudge: Not quite. In each pair, is someone staying put or going somewhere?
discover.reveal: Staying put takes the ablative (-ā, -ō). Going into or towards takes the receiver ending (-am, -um), as if the place receives you. The little words that go with each:

blocks.text: The ablative -ā looks like the doer -a. Only the macron (a long vowel) tells them apart, which is why textbooks print macrons. Roman inscriptions had none: context did the work.
Spanish con and en come from Latin cum and in. Latin mēcum (with me) survives in Spanish conmigo, which says "with" twice: con + migo.

blocks.title: in + ablative or receiver
blocks.note: Same little word, two meanings. The ending decides: -ā means in (staying), -am means into or to (going).

blocks.text: Julius Caesar invaded Britain twice, in 55 and 54 BC, and wrote about his campaigns himself in the Gallic War, the book generations of Latin students start with. You'll read its famous first line in the scenario.

phrases.es: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs.
phrases.en: All Gaul is divided into three parts.

exercises.why: Est means he's staying put: in + ablative, vīllā.
They work in the town, staying put: oppidō.
Ad takes the receiver ending: ad templum.

answer: i am walking with a friend
i am walking with my friend
exercises.why: Cum (with) + ablative amīcō. Ambulō: I walk.

exercises.prompt: Tap the word that is wrong.
exercises.why: Ad (towards) takes the receiver ending: templum.
In + Britanniam (-am): going to. Nāvigāmus: we sail.

exercises.prompt: Spanish conmigo (with me) comes from Latin…
exercises.why: Mēcum, with cum stuck on the end. Spanish later added con at the front too.
Living somewhere is staying put: in + ablative, Hispāniā. Habitāmus: we live.

exercises.prompt: Caesar opens the Gallic War with this line. Into how many parts is Gaul divided?
exercises.q: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs.
exercises.why: Trēs is three, like Spanish tres. Caesar goes on to name the peoples of each part.
Ā (from) takes the ablative: ā Rōmā. Venit: he comes.

answer: they walk out of the town
they are walking out of the town
they are walking out of town

exercises.prompt: Tap the word that is wrong.
exercises.why: Sumus means staying put, so in + ablative: in vīllā.

write.title: Write it in Latin
write.task: Write three Latin sentences about a journey: where you are, where you're going, and who you're with.
write.model: In Hispāniā sum. Ad oppidum ambulō. Cum amīcō in Galliam nāvigō.

boss.title: Reading: Caesar's Gaul
boss.persona: You are Magistra Līvia, a warm Latin teacher who loves Julius Caesar's Gallic War. The learner knows the present tense, nouns in -a, -us and -um as doer, receiver and ablative, and in, ad, ex, ā, cum. Chat in English about Caesar, Gaul and Britain, and give very short Latin sentences in Caesar's style for them to read, gently glossing any new word.

turns.npc: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs.
turns.en: omnis = all, dīvīsa = divided, partēs trēs = three parts
choices: All Gaul is divided into three parts.
Gaul is divided into many parts.
Trēs is three: think Spanish tres.
All Italy is divided into three parts.
Gallia is Gaul, roughly modern France.

turns.npc: Belgae, Aquītānī et Celtae in Galliā habitant.
choices: The Belgae, the Aquitani and the Celts live in Gaul.
The Belgae and the Aquitani live in Italy.
In Galliā: in Gaul.
The Belgae, the Aquitani and the Celts are moving into Gaul.
Galliā ends in -ā: staying put, so they live there.

turns.npc: Caesar cum mīlitibus in Galliam venit.
choices: Caesar comes into Gaul with soldiers.
Caesar comes out of Gaul with soldiers.
In + Galliam (-am) means into. Out of would be ex Galliā.
Caesar is in Gaul with soldiers.
Galliam ends in -am: going into, not staying.
Afterwards he sails to Britain.
Afterwards he sails from Britain.
From would be ā Britanniā. In + -am means to or into.
Afterwards they sail to Britain.
Nāvigat ends in -t: he. They would be -nt.

boss.chatOpeningEn: What do you know about Caesar? Ask me anything about him, or try a sentence in Latin.
